The Mayor's two letters:
AI adoption, unemployment,
and Cape Town's wager.

In the same week, Geordin Hill-Lewis sent a letter about 33.6% unemployment demanding national urgency — and announced that city managers will not receive salary increases unless they demonstrate AI adoption. Both positions are defensible. The tension between them deserves more than a headline.

Jarrit Hosking
Forge Vertical · Cape Town · September 1, 2026
10 min read
// The context

Two documents from the same desk, roughly the same week.

The first: a letter published under DA Leader Geordin Hill-Lewis's name, sent to supporters on August 24, 2026. Its subject is South Africa's unemployment crisis. The latest official statistics show unemployment rose to 33.6% in the second quarter of this year. Among young people, unemployment is now 47.4%. There are now around 8.5 million South Africans actively looking for work. The letter demands urgency. It calls out incrementalism. It says South Africa cannot afford to crawl forward.

The second: a statement made at the BizNews Conference on August 11, 2026, reported widely. City of Cape Town mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis said he would not grant the metro's departmental managers' additional budget for salaries unless they implemented artificial intelligence in their operations. "I will not even consider a salary proposal or request that comes to me unless you can demonstrate how you are introducing AI adoption and automation in your department," he said.

Both are from the same person. Both reflect a coherent strategic vision. And they sit in a tension that neither document acknowledges — because the honest question raised by reading them together is this: if AI makes government departments more efficient with fewer people, and 47.4% of young South Africans are already unemployed, what exactly is the plan for the people on the other side of that efficiency?

What Hill-Lewis is actually doing

// Chapter 01 — The logic of the policy

To be fair to the Mayor, the AI adoption policy is not reckless. It is a specific response to a specific problem: government bureaucracy expanding by default, with salary budget requests arriving regularly and justified by workload rather than efficiency gains.

Hill-Lewis said he was really firm about refusing requests to avoid the city bureaucracy expanding. He has been accommodating requests that met one key condition over the last year — demonstrating how the department is introducing AI adoption and automation. The condition is not "automate everything." It is "show me you are thinking about efficiency before asking for more money." That is a reasonable managerial position.

Cape Town already uses AI in several areas. The city has tested traffic cameras that can detect drivers using cellphones or not wearing seatbelts. It has also launched Maya, an AI-powered service to help global investors. Maya is available 24 hours a day in eight languages, including Afrikaans and Xhosa, and serves as a single-entry point into Cape Town's investment ecosystem. It helps investors navigate municipal processes, identify opportunities, access business support programmes and connect with City officials.

Cape Town is ranked first in Counterpoint Research's 2026 Africa AI Cities Index. South Africa ranks 46th out of 147 economies in Microsoft's 2026 Global AI Diffusion Report, emerging as Africa's most AI-ready economy. The ambition is real and the early infrastructure is real. The Mayor is not performing interest in AI — he is embedding it into budget governance.

"I've said I will not even consider a salary proposal or request that comes to me unless you can demonstrate how you are introducing AI adoption and automation in your department." — Geordin Hill-Lewis, BizNews Conference, August 11, 2026

The question neither letter asks

// Chapter 02 — The tension in plain language

The unemployment letter is correct about South Africa's crisis. The AI adoption policy is correct as a managerial tool. Neither document acknowledges what happens when you apply the second to a country living inside the first.

Government employment in South Africa is not just employment. For many households — particularly in communities where private sector jobs are scarce or non-existent — a municipal job is the single most reliable income source available. The City of Cape Town employs around 30,000 people. When efficiency means fewer of those jobs exist, or that existing jobs are restructured around AI-assisted workflows, the downstream impact lands on communities that have no fallback.

Only 26% of South African households have a computer at home, while more than 11,000 public schools lack a computer centre. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in business and public services, wider access to devices and digital skills will be essential if the economic opportunities created by this technology are to benefit all South Africans.

This is the digital divide problem inside the AI adoption problem inside the unemployment problem. They are not separate issues. A city that becomes more AI-efficient without a parallel programme to retrain and redeploy the humans displaced by that efficiency is not solving unemployment — it is concentrating it.

Government employment in South Africa is not just employment. For many households it is the only reliable income source within reach. Efficiency without a transition plan is not reform. It is cost-cutting with better branding.

The case for the Mayor's position

// Chapter 03 — Steel-manning the approach

The counterargument is worth making properly.

The alternative to AI-efficient government is not more government jobs. It is a bloated, slow-moving bureaucracy that costs more, delivers less, and cannot attract the private investment that creates the private sector jobs South Africa actually needs at scale. A city that cannot process a building permit efficiently, respond to a service delivery complaint quickly, or handle investor queries without a human in the loop for every step is not a competitive city. And competitive cities are where jobs come from.

The unemployment letter makes exactly this point: if infrastructure works, investment follows. If businesses invest and grow, they hire people. The AI-efficient city is the precondition for the investment-attracting city is the precondition for the job-creating city. The logic is not incoherent. It is sequential.

The question is whether the sequence moves fast enough for the 8.5 million people searching for work now. And whether the transition — from old government employment models to new ones — is being planned at the same urgency as the AI adoption itself.

What is missing from both documents: A transition plan. The unemployment letter demands urgency on reform without specifying what happens to people currently employed in the roles being automated. The AI adoption policy sets a condition for salary increases without specifying what reskilling support is available to departments asked to change how they work. Both documents diagnose the problem correctly. Neither describes what the city does with the people caught between the old model and the new one.

What Cape Town's AI ambition actually requires

// Chapter 04 — The infrastructure question

There is a version of AI-enabled Cape Town that works well for everyone. It is not the version where government becomes more efficient by quietly reducing headcount. It is the version where government becomes more efficient by redeploying people into higher-value work — and where the efficiency gains are reinvested in the services that underserved communities actually need.

That version requires digital infrastructure that does not yet exist at scale. The broader campaign is supported by a planned R120 billion infrastructure investment programme over the next decade, covering water security and energy resilience required for economic growth. The infrastructure spend is real. The question is whether digital skills development — not just broadband access, but genuine AI literacy for the workforce and the public — is being treated with the same seriousness.

task-bridge — the open protocol Forge Vertical has been developing — is one answer to a specific part of this problem. If AI systems are going to generate work signals that require human validation and execution, those signals need to reach humans who can respond to them. That requires people with digital skills and a platform that connects them to the work. The Merge Café concept — physical spaces where human capability and AI scale meet — is a model for what Cape Town's AI transition could look like at the community level, not just the managerial level.

The Mayor is thinking correctly about efficiency. The next question — and the harder one — is about equity. How do you build an AI-enabled city in a country where 47.4% of young people are unemployed, without the AI adoption itself becoming another mechanism that concentrates opportunity in the hands of people who already have access to it?

Seven questions the documents don't answer

// Chapter 05 — What to watch
01
What is the reskilling plan for departments asked to adopt AI?
The condition is clear — adopt AI or no salary increase. What support is the City providing to departments that want to comply but lack the skills to do so?
02
How are efficiency gains being reinvested?
If AI adoption reduces the cost of delivering a service, where does that saving go? Back into the fiscus? Into services for underserved communities? Into digital infrastructure?
03
What happens to the employees whose roles change?
AI adoption in a department rarely means nothing changes for the people in that department. What is the City's policy on role transitions, redeployment, and support for affected staff?
04
Is Maya serving investors or residents?
Maya is designed to help global investors navigate Cape Town's investment ecosystem. It is available in eight languages. Who is the intended beneficiary — global capital or local residents?
05
How does a city ranked #1 in Africa for AI serve a population where 74% of households have no computer?
The AI Cities Index measures infrastructure and adoption at the city level. It does not measure whether that AI capability reaches the households that need it most.
06
What is the measurable definition of "AI adoption" for a department?
The policy says demonstrate AI adoption. What counts? A chatbot on a website? Predictive analytics in traffic management? A PowerPoint about AI strategy? The standard matters enormously.
07
Is Cape Town building AI capacity for itself or for South Africa?
Cape Town consistently outperforms the national average on most indicators. The risk is that AI adoption accelerates that divergence — making Cape Town more competitive while the rest of the country falls further behind.

The honest position

// Chapter 06 — Where this lands

Hill-Lewis is right that South Africa cannot afford incrementalism. He is right that AI adoption in government is necessary and overdue. He is right that leadership resistance to AI is a real obstacle that requires a real response. Tying salary increases to demonstrated adoption is a blunt instrument but it is a real instrument — and the absence of any instrument produces the traditional speed of government he correctly identifies as the problem.

The problem is not the AI adoption policy. The problem is the silence around its edges. A policy this consequential in a city this unequal, at a moment when national unemployment is 33.6% and rising, needs to be accompanied by an explicit equity framework. Who benefits from the efficiency? Who transitions out of roles that no longer exist? What does the City do when the humans who are most affected by AI adoption are the ones least able to participate in the AI economy?

The Mayor sent two letters in one week. One was about urgency. The other was about transformation. They are not contradictory — but they are incomplete without a third letter. The one that explains what happens to the 8.5 million people who are not city managers, not global investors, not AI-ready, and who are watching both of those letters from the outside wondering which one is for them.

A note from Forge Vertical: task-bridge is an open protocol being developed to route AI-displaced work back to humans — creating a signal economy where AI identifies tasks requiring human validation and pays people directly for that validation. It is one proposed answer to the equity gap this article describes. If you are building in this space or thinking about it, the GitHub is open and the manifesto is on this site.
